doc.title: Cascadu interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, November 15, 2019

chapter: Following the drum to New York
title: Frankie Malabe and recognizing Montego Joe from the dream
summary: In New York he studies with Frankie Malabe, goes to a batá performance, and recognizes Montego Joe as a man from his dream.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: he was leading a drum circle, whether he had a gig that night at the club, etcetera. I was attached to Emile’s drums. Drum in tow and we went. And I left there a month later after I had had a vision and a dream that there was this entire, this entire lineage of drummers that I was supposed to come into contact with on my path. And I saw them all, Monk, I saw every single one of them in the dream, who I would have to connect with. And I told Emile, I got up and I told Emile about the dream. And Emile said, “Brother, it’s time for you to go. You’ve got to get to those people.” And I left. I left, and from Emile I went to New York. And I had, I went to take a lesson at Drummers’ Collective in New York. And the lesson I had — I didn’t even know who the guy was. His name was Frankie Malabe, one of the, at the time one of the greatest congeros. Amazing, amazing conga, batá, percussion player. And I’m sitting down there with Frankie, the drums between us, Frankie is like sitting where you are, I’m sitting here, and there’s just drums between us etcetera, right? And before Frankie does anything, Frankie says to me, “What is it that you’re looking for?” He says, “Because you’re on a mission. You are on a spiritual mission.” This is how I connected with Frankie. And I said, I was shaking because I had never sat in the presence of someone who told me something about what came deeply into my consciousness, you know, as part of my journey. And so Frankie says, you know, “You have to study this drum.” He says, “We’re going to start here but I am doing a gig this weekend and I want you to come.” So I told him, I told him, I said, “I have to follow the sound of batá.” He says, “Come to the gig.” I go to this gig and it is the first time I am in the presence of batá players, right? Full on ceremonial dancing, and everything, it’s at the McBurney Y on 23rd Street in New York etcetera, it’s a performance, right? But the dancers are ceremonially dressed and everything else. I mean I had had experiences in Trinidad, but this was different, right? I’m in a different headspace now. And Frankie introduces me to another, to the gentleman who had actually put on the entire performance, right? I got introduced and of course I’m wowed by the batá and everything else, completely, completely, completely. The dancers, you know, Elegbara, Yemonja, with the divinities of dancing and everything else. And I get introduced to this gentleman and I told him that I’m being in New York and I want to study. I’m looking for a teacher. So he says, “Well you know, come over to my studio,” you know, on Monday, etcetera. I go over to his studio and I’m sitting down and we’re sitting down and again, Monk, like where you are sitting, and there is drums between us, right? And I’m here. And I’m getting ready and I’m looking down at the drums and then I look up. And I see this guy’s face as one of the guys that I saw in my dream. And I shouted out, “Stop! Stop! Stop! Don’t move.” I’m freaking out, right? I’m completely freaked out at this point in time. I’m like sitting there, and I’m like don’t move. Tears are welling up, my whole face has gone, I’m in this other place altogether. Right? And I’m sitting there and I’m like “Don’t

move. Don’t move.” And tears are running down my face. And I said, “It’s you! It’s you, it’s you.” And I’m talking. “You, I saw you in my dream. I saw you in my dream, I saw you.” And it was Montego Joe you know? Montego was one of those classic Caribbean percussionists, man, who had made it sort of on the big stage with guys like Babatunde Olatunji and, you know, Chief Bey, and you know, I mean it was that era, like the 50s, 60s, etcetera, and Montego was one of those musicians who had played, you know as a percussionist, he was a drummer, you know a set player, he played set and everything else. He toured with Hamiet Bluiett and all these guys and everything, and I’m sitting there with the guy. I don’t know him, I don’t know anything about him, I just know that I saw you in my dream, you’re the one, don’t move, don’t say a word.
How did he react to that?
